View in browser             Sponsored by       Jacob Passy   What It Takes to Get a ‘Free’ Casino Cruise   Plus, United Airlines’ AI ban and Thanksgiving travel projections   Happy Friday! This is WSJ travel reporter Jacob Passy, filling in again for Dawn Gilbertson. Here in New York it’s beginning to look like Christmas. Holiday markets are already in full swing in Bryant Park and Grand Central Station, and decorations are popping up everywhere. 

   In travel news, United Airlines has banned AI assistants from making flight bookings, citing data-privacy concerns. Travel is emerging as one of the top use-cases for AI agents like Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots. Have you used one of these bots to book a trip yet? 

   Alaska Airlines is introducing Atmos Global Concierge, a new, invite-only status level similar to United’s Global Services, American’s Concierge Key and Delta’s 360 status. 

   Google agreed to more stringent privacy protections related to information pertaining to former Spirit Airlines employees in its bid to buy data from the bankrupt company. Australian airline Qantas is laying off around 850 workers after signing a deal with Accenture that the carrier says will modernize its systems.  

   Protests in Spain tied to the country’s first general strike in over a decade disrupted cruise ports and public transportation. 

       High rolling on the high seas     JEFF LAUTENBERGER FOR WSJ   For some, the holy grail of vacation deals is the free-cruise offer. Who wouldn’t want to visit the Caribbean or Mexico without spending a dime?

   For many cruise aficionados, the casino is their ticket to the vacations of their dreams. If you’ve been on a cruise, chances are you’ve met someone who was ostensibly sailing on the casino’s dime. Online forums and social media are filled with people boasting of the offers flooding their inboxes, like this TikTok user who planned to cruise for six months through casino-related comps he received.

   Perhaps unsurprisingly, gambling in the ship’s casino isn’t a foolproof way of getting a free cruise. As Colleen McDaniel, editor in chief of Cruise Critic, told me: “The formula isn’t so cut-and-dried.”

   Each cruise line has its own casino loyalty program—generally separate from the line’s regular loyalty program—that tracks your activity at table games and slot machines. 

   You earn points based on how much you wager, including money you put into the machines as well as any winnings you re-wager. “The casino offer is based on how much you play, rather than how much you win or lose,” McDaniel said.

   At Carnival, for instance, Players Club members earn one point for every $2 coined in on slots or every $5 wagered in video poker. Table-game earnings are based on the game played, how long a person remains at the table and the average bet sizes. 

   So how many points does it take to earn a free cruise? With Royal Caribbean’s Club Royale casino program, for instance, you have to accrue at least 2,500 points to reach the Prime tier. This status comes with an annual free cruise in an interior stateroom. (Additional cruise offers may come your way, and higher tiers entitle you to nicer cabins.)

   Tanner Callais, founder of cruise website Cruzely, said he’s never received a free cruise offer based on his gambling. “But I’m a low-stakes player,” he said.

   This summer, my husband and I went on back-to-back cruises with Royal Caribbean and Norwegian. We’re not big gamblers—only wagering around $100 each night between the two of us— and by the end of our trip we were actually up a small chunk. Within a couple of months, we got our first cruise offer from Royal Caribbean. So far, no such luck with Norwegian.

   Of course, free is in the eye of the beholder. Aside from what a person might lose playing, the cruise offers don’t cover the cost of taxes and port fees. 

   “If you are someone who likes to gamble, then by all means take advantage by tracking your play,” Callais advised. “Just like on land, however, those comps are likely to be more than paid for by what you’d expect to lose from gambling.”

If you create a collection for the videos you bookmark related to your getaway, you can share that collection with the rest of your party to nail down your itinerary together.

       Travel Math 🧮   29 million   The number of passengers lobbying group Airlines for America expects U.S. carriers to serve over the Thanksgiving holiday period. Airlines have upped their capacity for this year’s holiday, despite fuel prices and fares.

       And We Quote 💬   “I don’t think fares are going to fall as much as people expect.”

   — JetBlue CEO Joanna Geraghty, in an interview with CNBC about how the cost of flights will respond to a potential drop in fuel prices .

       In My Carry-on 👜     JACOB PASSY/WSJ   For Bruce Poon Tip, founder of tour company G Adventures, getting shut-eye on the go can be a challenge, especially when hopping across time zones.

   His carry-on—a backpack that never leaves his side when traveling—is filled with tools meant to help him sleep. Those include over-the-counter options like melatonin as well as prescription medications.

   But no matter where he’s sleeping, he’ll wear his Ozlo Sleepbuds. The device features built-in white noise and has the ability to shift between sounds to help you wake up when the time comes. It was especially handy during a recent trip to Europe for a conference.

   “I landed in the morning, and I had to be on stage at 11,” he said. “I couldn’t be a wreck, so I had to make sure I slept on the plane.”

What It Takes to Get a ‘Free’ Casino Cruise
 
Plus, United Airlines’ AI ban and Thanksgiving travel projections
 

Happy Friday! This is WSJ travel reporter Jacob Passy, filling in again for Dawn Gilbertson. Here in New York it’s beginning to look like Christmas. Holiday markets are already in full swing in Bryant Park and Grand Central Station, and decorations are popping up everywhere.

 

In travel news, United Airlines has banned AI assistants from making flight bookings, citing data-privacy concerns. Travel is emerging as one of the top use-cases for AI agents like Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots. Have you used one of these bots to book a trip yet?

 

Alaska Airlines is introducing Atmos Global Concierge, a new, invite-only status level similar to United’s Global Services, American’s Concierge Key and Delta’s 360 status.

 

Google agreed to more stringent privacy protections related to information pertaining to former Spirit Airlines employees in its bid to buy data from the bankrupt company. Australian airline Qantas is laying off around 850 workers after signing a deal with Accenture that the carrier says will modernize its systems. 

 

Protests in Spain tied to the country’s first general strike in over a decade disrupted cruise ports and public transportation.

 
 
 

High rolling on the high seas

 
 
JEFF LAUTENBERGER FOR WSJ
 

For some, the holy grail of vacation deals is the free-cruise offer. Who wouldn’t want to visit the Caribbean or Mexico without spending a dime?

 

For many cruise aficionados, the casino is their ticket to the vacations of their dreams. If you’ve been on a cruise, chances are you’ve met someone who was ostensibly sailing on the casino’s dime. Online forums and social media are filled with people boasting of the offers flooding their inboxes, like this TikTok user who planned to cruise for six months through casino-related comps he received.

 

Perhaps unsurprisingly, gambling in the ship’s casino isn’t a foolproof way of getting a free cruise. As Colleen McDaniel, editor in chief of Cruise Critic, told me: “The formula isn’t so cut-and-dried.”

 

Each cruise line has its own casino loyalty program—generally separate from the line’s regular loyalty program—that tracks your activity at table games and slot machines. 

 

You earn points based on how much you wager, including money you put into the machines as well as any winnings you re-wager. “The casino offer is based on how much you play, rather than how much you win or lose,” McDaniel said.

 

At Carnival, for instance, Players Club members earn one point for every $2 coined in on slots or every $5 wagered in video poker. Table-game earnings are based on the game played, how long a person remains at the table and the average bet sizes. 

 

So how many points does it take to earn a free cruise? With Royal Caribbean’s Club Royale casino program, for instance, you have to accrue at least 2,500 points to reach the Prime tier. This status comes with an annual free cruise in an interior stateroom. (Additional cruise offers may come your way, and higher tiers entitle you to nicer cabins.)

 

Tanner Callais, founder of cruise website Cruzely, said he’s never received a free cruise offer based on his gambling. “But I’m a low-stakes player,” he said.

 

This summer, my husband and I went on back-to-back cruises with Royal Caribbean and Norwegian. We’re not big gamblers—only wagering around $100 each night between the two of us— and by the end of our trip we were actually up a small chunk. Within a couple of months, we got our first cruise offer from Royal Caribbean. So far, no such luck with Norwegian.

 

Of course, free is in the eye of the beholder. Aside from what a person might lose playing, the cruise offers don’t cover the cost of taxes and port fees. 

 

“If you are someone who likes to gamble, then by all means take advantage by tracking your play,” Callais advised. “Just like on land, however, those comps are likely to be more than paid for by what you’d expect to lose from gambling.”

In My Carry-on 👜

 
 
JACOB PASSY/WSJ
 

For Bruce Poon Tip, founder of tour company G Adventures, getting shut-eye on the go can be a challenge, especially when hopping across time zones.

 

His carry-on—a backpack that never leaves his side when traveling—is filled with tools meant to help him sleep. Those include over-the-counter options like melatonin as well as prescription medications.

 

But no matter where he’s sleeping, he’ll wear his Ozlo Sleepbuds. The device features built-in white noise and has the ability to shift between sounds to help you wake up when the time comes. It was especially handy during a recent trip to Europe for a conference.

 

“I landed in the morning, and I had to be on stage at 11,” he said. “I couldn’t be a wreck, so I had to make sure I slept on the plane.”
